Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
35-year-old lawyer with several weeks of new episodic frontal headaches, palpitations, heat intolerance, weight loss, arm paresthesias, and reduced libido that began after starting a higher-stress job; thyroid over-replacement and/or stress-related disorder most likely.

History:
• Presenting complaints: Severe frontal headaches, palpitations, feeling “hot,” episodic shortness of breath, bilateral arm tingling, reduced appetite with 5 lb unintentional weight loss, ↓ libido.  
• Onset/duration: All symptoms started after changing jobs (exact date not provided); occur mainly during work hours.  
• Course/triggers: Headaches and other symptoms often while at computer or in meetings; palpitations ~1×/day, sometimes in elevator or at desk; no exercise-induced dyspnea.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild nausea with headaches; no visual aura, no leg tingling, no exercise intolerance.  
• Pertinent negatives: No prior headache history, no smoking, no recreational drug use.  
• Past medical history: Thyroid disorder (patient states “hyperthyroidism”) on thyroxine replacement. No other chronic conditions reported.  
• Medications: Thyroxine (dose not specified).  
• Allergies: Not stated.  
• Social / preventive: Drinks wine once/week (2 glasses). Non-smoker. Lawyer in London; job stress rated 7–8/10. No illicit drugs.

Examination:
• Tele-visit only; no vitals or physical exam performed.

Impression:
1. Possible iatrogenic hyperthyroidism from excessive thyroxine replacement – compatible with heat intolerance, weight loss, palpitations, ↓ libido, episodic SOB/paresthesias.  
2. Stress-related / anxiety-panic episodes with tension-type headaches – temporal link to new high-stress job; autonomic symptoms (palpitations, SOB, tingling) and appetite/libido changes support.  
3. Primary tension or migraine-type headaches exacerbated by screen work – frontal location and mild nausea, but does not explain all systemic findings.

Plan:
• Arrange in-person clinic appointment for full physical examination (cardiac, respiratory, neurologic).  
• Order laboratory studies: thyroid panel (TSH, free T4/T3), CBC, electrolytes, glucose, B12, and possibly cortisol if indicated.  
• Consider ECG to evaluate palpitations.  
• No new medications until evaluation complete.  
• Advise patient on booking appointment via app; clinician will forward today’s history to clinic team.  
• Discuss stress management strategies at follow-up once organic causes addressed.  
• Safety-net: Seek urgent care if severe persistent headache, syncope, chest pain, or neurologic deficit develops.

Quality checks:

● Missing / expected elements: Exact symptom onset/date; complete allergy history; thyroxine dose & adherence details; family history; vitals; physical exam findings; follow-up timeframe/date.  
● Conflicts: Patient states “hyperthyroidism” yet is prescribed thyroxine (typically for hypothyroidism) – needs clarification.  
● Transcript quality: Acceptable but incomplete; several questions unanswered or partially answered, some conversational interruptions; no objective data obtained.
